prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks into persistent credit cycles

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) identified a dynamic mechanism. Borrowing limits tied to collateral, together with the asset prices that collateral values depend on, turn small and temporary shocks into large, persistent fluctuations. The result is a conceptual advance, not a modelling convenience. It is now the standard way macroeconomics, corporate finance and policy modelling represent financial frictions, and its relevance was reinforced by 2008. It is nearly three decades old, so its robustness and reach can be judged. Credit for the originating idea is concentrated in two people. A single-part, two-laureate award therefore fits the three-person limit cleanly and avoids forcing an arbitrary cut. I considered adding Autor from B044 as a second part, since he is central to both labour-demand strands. I decided against it. A one-name part would split the credit for the China-shock work from Hanson and Dorn, and it would misrepresent that achievement. I keep B044 as my first alternative because of its scientific strength, not as a hedge.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises may be thought to cover this territory. Direct empirical identification of the collateral-amplification mechanism is also weaker than the theory's influence suggests. The contribution rests on essentially one seminal paper and its extensions, which could be judged narrow next to the broader empirical programmes in B044 or B002. I have also had to qualify my opening wording. The Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist financial accelerator is a related and partly overlapping strand. Only Bernanke is a laureate, and he was recognised for the 2022 work on banks and crises. Gertler and Gilchrist have not been recognised. So the case for excluding them rests on the independent origin and distinctness of the collateral-constraint mechanism. It does not rest on prior recognition of the accelerator.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B040 first as a foundational macro-finance mechanism. He flags overlap with the 2022 prize, mixed direct empirical validation, and whether Gertler or Gilchrist should be added.
responses.response: I agree on the core attribution but want to be more precise on the overlap. The 2022 prize recognised bank runs, deposit-insurance theory and the empirical study of bank failures in depressions. Kiyotaki-Moore is a different mechanism, in which collateral values and asset prices create a feedback loop in the real economy. I accept that the empirical identification is less direct than the theory's influence. That is a real weakness, but it is common to foundational macro mechanisms. Influence on quantitative models and policy analysis is the better test of durability here. On Gertler and Gilchrist, I would keep the award to the originators. Their strand is the related financial accelerator, with its own empirical contributions. It should not be folded into a two-name credit for the 1997 mechanism.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B002 (Chetty, Hendren) first for its population-scale measurement and causal neighbourhood-effects evidence, and ranks B040 fourth. He notes that the empirical validation of B040 is more indirect and that Bernanke's earlier recognition complicates the framing.
responses.response: I take the point that B002 changed what can be measured, and I rank it highly. The causal-place results also still lack long-run replication and external validity outside the US, which I put under maturity, not novelty. I would not rank empirical directness above conceptual generality. A mechanism that reorganised how a whole field models credit and shocks is at least as strong a basis as a measurement advance. On the Bernanke point, I agree it affects how the committee should frame the citation. That is why I tie the citation to the collateral-constraint mechanism and do not use a wider 'financial frictions' wording. I would revisit B002 as the preferred choice if colleagues show the neighbourhood-effect estimates are robust over longer horizons.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B044 first and proposes Autor and Hanson as the cleanest attribution. He rates the work very highly, credits the combination of task-based theory with credible quasi-experimental evidence, and notes that identification relies on shift-share designs with known inference issues.
responses.response: I largely agree with the scientific assessment, and B044 is my second choice with the same pair. We differ on two points. First, the task-based framework and the China-shock evidence are separable strands with different co-authors (Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu, Katz in the first; Dorn in the second). The committee would have to decide whether they form one prize-sized achievement, and the three-person cap makes that decision costly. Dorn would be omitted from the central China-shock papers. Second, the shift-share inference issues and the debate over persistence and magnitude are still active, so I judge B040 to be less exposed on maturity. I do not think support counts settle this. If the committee decides the trade-shock evidence is the achievement and excludes the broader task framework, my reservation about B044 weakens considerably.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises to cover this territory closely enough to reduce the marginal case for B040.
Whether the committee should add Gertler or Gilchrist, which would bring in the financial-accelerator strand, or keep the credit to the originators of the collateral-constraint mechanism.
Whether the task-based labour-demand and China-shock strands in B044 count as one achievement or two, and how Dorn and Katz should be treated under the three-person cap.
How much weight indirect empirical validation should carry against conceptual generality and demonstrated influence on quantitative and policy models.
I have not independently verified the citation counts or the details of attribution used here.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Kiyotaki, Moore, Autor, Hanson or the other credited names is apparent from my supplied profile. My research is in macroeconomics, in the same broad field as B040. I have co-authored with committee colleagues Boppart and Friberg, and with the secretary Krusell, who is also an IIES colleague. None of these ties concerns the candidates in my preferred configuration, but I disclose them without adjudicating them.
